q: In 1996 Southampton boss Graeme Souness took a call from a man claiming to be George Weah, recommending his cousin. Which player did Souness sign, and how long did his Premier League career last?
a: Ali Dia, 53 minutes as a substitute against Leeds before being substituted himself

q: At the 1994 Caribbean Cup a golden goal in extra time counted double. Barbados led Grenada 2-1 with three minutes left but needed to win by two. What did they do?
a: Deliberately scored an own goal to make it 2-2 and force extra time, then won 4-2

q: Referee Ken Aston invented the yellow and red card after a language mix-up at the 1966 World Cup. What gave him the idea on the drive home?
a: Traffic lights, on Kensington High Street

q: Which 1962 World Cup game did the BBC's David Coleman introduce as the most stupid, appalling, disgusting and disgraceful exhibition of football possibly in the history of the game?
a: Chile against Italy, the Battle of Santiago

q: Arbroath beat Bon Accord 36-0 in the 1885 Scottish Cup. What was the Arbroath goalkeeper doing for most of it?
a: Sheltering under an umbrella he borrowed from a spectator, he never touched the ball

q: Arbroath's 36-0 was not even a clear winner as the score of the day. Which club won 35-0 the same afternoon in 1885?
a: Dundee Harp, against Aberdeen Rovers

q: Scotland kicked off a World Cup qualifier in Tallinn in 1996 and the referee blew for full time after three seconds. Why?
a: Estonia never turned up, after a row over the floodlights had moved the kick-off time

q: After the Dutch knocked West Germany out in Hamburg at Euro 88, what did Ronald Koeman do with the shirt he had swapped with Olaf Thon?
a: Pretended to wipe his backside with it, in front of the Dutch fans

q: In August 1973 the Ajax squad held a secret ballot for the captaincy, and weeks later Johan Cruyff was gone to Barcelona. Who had beaten him to the armband?
a: Piet Keizer

q: Feyenoord changed the spelling of its own name in 1974. What was it before, and why did they bother?
a: Feijenoord, because foreigners could not pronounce the Dutch ij

q: In 1925 the Spanish government shut Barcelona's ground for months and forced founder Joan Gamper out of the club. What had the crowd done?
a: Jeered the Spanish national anthem

q: On a Real Madrid tour in 1963, Alfredo Di Stéfano was taken from his hotel at six in the morning by guerrillas and held for three days. In which city?
a: Caracas

q: UD Las Palmas did not grow, it was assembled. How many Gran Canaria clubs merged in 1949 to create it?
a: Five

q: Founded in 1949 in the third tier, Las Palmas hold a record no other Spanish club has. What did they manage in their first two seasons?
a: Back to back promotions, reaching La Liga two years after being founded

q: Real Oviedo needed nearly two million euros in two weeks in 2012 or they were finished. What saved them?
a: Fans around the world buying 11 euro shares, which then persuaded Carlos Slim to invest

q: Goalkeeper Rogério Ceni scored 131 goals for São Paulo, a world record. How many of them came from open play?
a: One, the rest were free kicks and penalties

q: The longest match on record, Stockport County against Doncaster Rovers in 1946, lasted three hours and 23 minutes. What finally stopped it?
a: Darkness, the ground had no floodlights

q: Graham Poll showed Josip Šimunić three yellow cards in one 2006 World Cup game. What was his explanation?
a: He had written the second booking down against an Australian player, because Šimunić sounded Australian

q: A Liverpool engineer patented the goal net in 1889 after watching a disallowed goal at Everton. What else did he later help build?
a: The Mersey road tunnel, he was John Alexander Brodie

q: The Euro 1968 semi-final between Italy and the Soviet Union finished goalless after 120 minutes. How was it decided?
a: A coin toss, which Italy's Giacinto Facchetti won by calling tails

q: Juventus played in pink until 1903, when an English player in the side wrote home for new shirts. Which club's colours turned up?
a: Notts County's black and white stripes

q: With the ball at his feet in the box and the Everton keeper down injured in 2000, what did Paolo Di Canio do?
a: Caught the ball so the keeper could be treated, and won the FIFA Fair Play award for it

q: In 2002 Norwegian club Flekkerøy signed striker Kenneth Kristensen for one kilo of seafood per kilo of player. What was the final fee?
a: 75 kilos of shrimp, weighed out at a boxing-style weigh-in

q: The joint manager who took Iceland to Euro 2016 and beat England had another job. What was it?
a: Dentist, Heimir Hallgrímsson still ran a practice

q: The Faroe Islands beat Austria 1-0 in their first ever competitive match in 1990. What was their goalkeeper Jens Martin Knudsen wearing?
a: A white bobble hat, which he had worn since a concussion at 13

q: Heerenveen trailed Ajax 5-1 with half an hour left on 7 May 1950 and won 6-5. Which Frisian folk hero dragged them back?
a: Abe Lenstra, who scored three

q: Ajax were thrown out of Europe for a year in 1989 after a UEFA Cup tie against Austria Wien was abandoned. What had been thrown at the Austrian keeper?
a: An iron rod, from the F-side

q: Go Ahead Eagles were founded in 1902 under a different English name. What was it before the Dutch FA made them change?
a: Be Quick

q: Go Ahead Eagles won the KNVB Cup in 2025, their first major trophy ever. Who did they beat, and how?
a: AZ, on penalties after a 1-1 draw

q: Uruguayan striker Sebastián Abreu holds a Guinness record no manager wants on a CV. What for?
a: Most clubs played for, more than 30

q: A three-match World Cup qualifier in 1969 helped tip two countries into a four day shooting war. Which two?
a: El Salvador and Honduras

q: Thomas Helmer's shot in 1994 went wide but was given as a goal, and Bayern beat Nürnberg. What did the German FA do about it?
a: Ordered the match replayed, and Bayern won that 5-0 as well

q: Manchester United came out for the second half at Southampton in 1996 in a different kit. What was Alex Ferguson's reason?
a: His players could not pick each other out in the grey shirts

q: Kanu did not realise the ball had been kicked out for an injury and set up Arsenal's winner against Sheffield United in the 1999 FA Cup. What did Arsène Wenger do?
a: Offered to replay the whole tie, and Arsenal won that 2-1 as well

q: Robbie Fowler won a UEFA Fair Play award in 1997 for telling the referee that David Seaman had not fouled him. How did it end?
a: The penalty stood, Seaman saved it, and Jason McAteer scored the rebound

q: England captain Bobby Moore was arrested in Bogotá in 1970 for stealing a bracelet. What killed the case against him?
a: The tracksuit he was accused of pocketing it in had no pockets

q: Garrincha won two World Cups with a body that should have stopped him. What was wrong with his legs?
a: Childhood polio left them bent, both knees pointing left and one leg shorter than the other

q: Before Argentina played Italy in Naples at the 1990 World Cup, what did Maradona ask the Neapolitans to remember?
a: That the rest of Italy did not treat them as Italians, so they should back Argentina

q: Barcelona were beaten 11-1 by Real Madrid in a 1943 cup semi-final after leading the tie 3-0. What had happened in their dressing room beforehand?
a: Franco's director of state security had come in to remind them they played only by the regime's generosity

q: Jan Jongbloed kept goal for the Netherlands in the 1974 and 1978 World Cup finals. Which shirt number did he wear?
At the 1978 World Cup a Dutch defender became the first man to score at both ends in the same World Cup match. Who?
a: Ernie Brandts, against Italy

q: Brian Clough turned up late to unveil Britain's first million pound player in 1979 carrying what?
a: A squash racket, and wearing a tracksuit, to play the whole thing down

q: Cameroon were fined and docked six qualifying points in 2004 over their kit. What was wrong with it?
a: It was a one piece bodysuit, and FIFA required shirt and shorts to be separate items

q: Mexico goalkeeper Jorge Campos wore neon kits he had designed himself. What else did he do that keepers do not?
a: Played as a forward, scoring 14 league goals in a season for Pumas

q: German goalkeeper Lutz Pfannenstiel spent 101 days in a Singapore prison and stopped breathing three times on a pitch in Bradford. What is he officially the only footballer to have done?
a: Played professionally in all six FIFA confederations

q: Who holds the record for the fastest booking in English football, carded three seconds into an FA Cup tie in 1992?
a: Vinnie Jones

q: Referee Damián Rubino set a Guinness record in an Argentine fourth division match in 2011. What for?
a: Sending off 36 players, every player and substitute from both sides

q: The 1923 FA Cup final, the first at Wembley, started 45 minutes late. Who is credited with clearing the pitch?
a: A police horse called Billie, and PC George Scorey

q: Japan's King Kazu, Kazuyoshi Miura, was still a registered professional at 58. Which Brazilian club did he start at in 1986?
a: Santos

q: Referee Clive Thomas never worked another World Cup after Brazil against Sweden in 1978. What did he do?
a: Blew for full time while a corner was in the air, disallowing Zico's header

q: The 2004 Manchester United win that ended Arsenal's 49 match unbeaten run has a nickname. What flew at Alex Ferguson in the tunnel?
a: A slice of pizza, hence the Battle of the Buffet

q: A women's club match at Goodison Park in 1920 drew 53,000, with thousands locked out. What did the FA do a year later?
a: Banned women from playing on the grounds of its member clubs, a ban that lasted until 1971

q: Celtic won the European Cup in 1967 with a squad that shared one unusual thing. What?
a: Every player was born within 30 miles of Celtic Park

q: Before settling on football, Lev Yashin was good enough at another sport to win a national cup in 1953. Which?
a: Ice hockey, as a goalkeeper for Dynamo Moscow

q: One man has played in two World Cup finals for two different countries. Who?
a: Luis Monti, for Argentina in 1930 and Italy in 1934

q: At Corinthians in the early 1980s, Sócrates and his teammates ran the club by vote. What were they voting on?
a: Everything, from the team selection to wages and travel, one man one vote including the kit man

q: The 1980 Copa del Rey final was a Madrid derby of an odd kind. Who did Real Madrid beat 6-1?
a: Real Madrid Castilla, their own reserve team

q: Ruud Gullit won the Ballon d'Or in 1987 and dedicated it to a man in prison. Who?
a: Nelson Mandela

q: The 2001 UEFA Cup final between Liverpool and Alavés finished 5-4 on a golden goal. Who scored it?
a: Delfí Geli of Alavés, into his own net

q: The 1994 World Cup opening ceremony ended with Diana Ross taking a penalty at a rigged goal. What happened?
a: She missed by a metre and the goal collapsed anyway

q: English referee Andy Wain abandoned a Sunday league match in 2005 after squaring up to a goalkeeper. What had he done first?
a: Sent himself off, saying he would have sent off any player who did that

q: Colombian midfielder Gerardo Bedoya holds a Guinness record for the wrong reasons. What is it?
a: Most red cards in a professional career, 46

q: Deportivo needed a last minute penalty on the final day of 1994 to win their first Spanish title. Who missed it?
a: Miroslav Djukić

q: A Seville derby in the 2007 Copa del Rey was abandoned and finished behind closed doors in Getafe. Why?
a: Sevilla coach Juande Ramos was knocked unconscious by a bottle thrown from the stand

q: Atlético Madrid were nearly bankrupt after the Spanish Civil War and merged with another club to survive. Who with?
a: Aviación Nacional, the air force club, making them Atlético Aviación

q: Spanish goalkeeper Ricardo Zamora was reported shot dead in 1936, then found alive in a Madrid prison. What is said to have kept him there?
a: Playing football with the guards, until the Argentine embassy got him out

q: When Athletic Bilbao win a major trophy they parade it in a way no other club does. How?
a: On a barge, the gabarra, down the river Nervión into Bilbao

q: Barcelona's motto més que un club was not invented by a marketing department. Who said it first, in 1968?
a: Club president Narcís de Carreras, in his nomination speech

q: After Cruyff's Barcelona won 5-0 at the Bernabéu in February 1974, what did Catalans keep saying to him instead of congratulations?
a: Thank you

q: Roger Milla was retired and playing on Réunion when he was talked back into the Cameroon squad for the 1990 World Cup. Who talked him round?
a: Paul Biya, the president of Cameroon, who phoned him

q: Nottingham Forest won back to back European Cups with a striker Brian Clough had bought for 2,000 pounds from Long Eaton United. What was his day job before that?
a: Carpet fitter, he was Garry Birtles

q: Ajax's heaviest ever home defeat in the league, 6-3 at De Meer in 1980, was handed to them by which club?
a: MVV Maastricht

q: In November 1973 Chile kicked off a World Cup play-off in an empty Estadio Nacional, walked the ball into the net and the referee ended it. Where was the other team?
a: The Soviet Union refused to play in a stadium Pinochet had used as a prison

q: After Norway beat England in 1981, commentator Bjørge Lillelien listed Lord Nelson, Churchill and Lady Diana before shouting one line at the British prime minister. What?
a: Maggie Thatcher, your boys took one hell of a beating

q: Iceland's thunderclap looks ancient but is not. Where did their fans pick it up?
a: From Motherwell fans, when Stjarnan played at Fir Park in 2014

q: Ajax's founders named the club after a Greek warrior for one specific reason. What was it?
a: Ajax killed himself rather than be beaten, so he died unconquered

q: Sparta Rotterdam's red and white stripes came from a board trip to England in 1899. Which club's kit did they copy?
a: Sunderland

q: Faas Wilkes was banned from the Dutch national team from 1949 to 1955 in his prime. What had he done wrong?
a: Turned professional abroad, which the amateur-only KNVB would not allow

q: On the last day of the 1999 season, Carlisle United needed a goal in the final seconds to stay in the Football League. Who scored it?
a: Their on-loan goalkeeper Jimmy Glass, who had come up for a corner

q: Real Madrid went into the final day one point clear in both 1992 and 1993, and lost the title both times to the same opponent. Who kept beating them?
a: Tenerife
